import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Combinatorial representation of the recurrence $a(n+2) = 2a(n+1) + 2a(n)$

A028859 (OEIS): $a(n+2) = 2 \cdot a(n+1) + 2 \cdot a(n)$; $a(0) = 1$, $a(1) = 3$.

*References:*
- [A028859](https://oeis.org/A028859)
- [arxiv/2605.22763](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22763) *Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search* by George Tsoukalas et al.
-/

namespace OeisA28859


/--
A028859 (OEIS): $a(n+2) = 2 \cdot a(n+1) + 2 \cdot a(n)$; $a(0) = 1$, $a(1) = 3$.
-/
def a (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  match n with
  | 0 => 1
  | 1 => 3
  | (n + 2) => 2 * a (n + 1) + 2 * a n
termination_by n

set_option linter.unusedVariables false


@[category test, AMS 11]
lemma a_0 : a 0 = 1 := by native_decide

@[category test, AMS 11]
lemma a_1 : a 1 = 3 := by native_decide

@[category test, AMS 11]
lemma a_2 : a 2 = 8 := by native_decide

@[category test, AMS 11]
lemma a_3 : a 3 = 22 := by native_decide

@[category test, AMS 11]
lemma a_4 : a 4 = 60 := by native_decide


/--
Conjecture: The sequence a(n) is also the number of compositions of $n$ into positive integers
such that adjacent parts and the largest part differ by at most 1. - _Gus Wiseman_, May 19 2020

A formal proof has been found with the methods described in
[arxiv/2605.22763](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22763).
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using formal_conjectures at
"https://github.com/mo271/formal-conjectures/blob/a32396489dcb8f86c3549b93aa358ac6a10a3a1f/FormalConjectures/OEIS/28859.wip.lean#L402"]
theorem exists_finset_sequence (n : ℕ) :
    let L := n + 1
    let Sequence := Fin L → ℕ
    let S : Set Sequence :=
      {σ : Sequence |
        L > 0 ∧
          (∀ i : Fin L, σ i > 0) ∧
            let max_val := Finset.sup Finset.univ σ
            (∀ k : ℕ, 1 ≤ k ∧ k ≤ max_val → ∃ i : Fin L, σ i = k) ∧
            (∀ i j : Fin L, i < j → j.val ≠ i.val + 1 → σ i ≥ σ j)}
    ∃ (F : Finset Sequence), (F : Set Sequence) = S ∧ F.card = a n := by
    sorry

end OeisA28859

findings.description: The docstring at lines 62–63 describes compositions of n whose adjacent parts and largest part differ by at most 1. This is not Wiseman's cited conjecture. The Lean correctly counts length-(n+1) positive-integer sequences with an initial-interval image and weakly decreasing non-adjacent pairs. Only the prose is wrong; adding a sum condition or changing the inequalities would damage the faithful statement.
findings.source_evidence: OEIS A028859, Gus Wiseman's May 19, 2020 comment: “Also the number of length n + 1 sequences that cover an initial interval of positive integers and whose non-adjacent parts are weakly decreasing.” Read through the official mirror at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/oeis/oeisdata/main/seq/A028/A028859.seq. Xinjun Wang's linked paper, Theorem 1, explicitly confirms this length-indexed interpretation: https://zenodo.org/records/20437247/files/A028859.pdf.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the first two docstring lines with: “The sequence $a(n)$ counts length-$(n+1)$ sequences of positive integers that cover an initial interval of positive integers and whose non-adjacent parts are weakly decreasing. Conjectured by Gus Wiseman, May 19, 2020.” Retain the Lean statement and solved status.

reformulations.difference: The source counts sequences covering an initial interval. Lean expresses this using positive-valued functions on Fin (n+1), coverage up to Finset.sup, and an existential Finset containing exactly all qualifying functions.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For positive length, M = Finset.univ.sup σ is the maximum entry. Positivity and the maximum bound put the image inside {1,…,M}; the coverage clause gives the reverse inclusion. The condition i < j and j.val ≠ i.val + 1 is equivalent to i.val + 1 < j.val, exactly non-adjacency in a linear sequence. Coverage also implies M ≤ n+1, since every integer 1,…,M occurs among n+1 entries. Thus the qualifying functions form a finite set, and the existential Finset/cardinality formulation is precisely the source's count. Both the predicate equivalence and the counting-statement equivalence were proved in /workspace/review/scratch.lean without sorryAx.

review.notes: All seven declarations were checked. The recurrence and five test lemmas match OEIS. Exhaustive Lean enumeration for n = 0,…,5 produced 1,3,8,22,60,164; at n = 0 the sole sequence is (1). OEIS records proofs by Wang and DeepMind, supporting the solved tag. The historical linked proof has the same statement and no explicit sorries/custom axioms. It was inspected but not freshly kernel-certified: recompilation with the current dependencies failed on legacy APIs/tactics. This does not establish a status defect. The ordinary OEIS page was blocked by Cloudflare, so its official data mirror was used. The target file was not modified.
